# OSMnx

Python library that downloads street networks from OpenStreetMap and hands them back as
[[networkx]] graphs, with the routing-relevant cleanup already done. Used in
[[optimization-methods]] as the only source of geography for [[multi-depot-vehicle-routing]] —
pinned as `osmnx>=2.0`, the one pinned dependency in `instance_generator/requirements.txt`.

## How it is used

```
graph_from_point(dist=5000, network_type="drive")
  → truncate.largest_component(strongly=True)
  → collapse parallel edges to the shortest directed length
  → CSV
```

- `network_type="drive"` keeps one-way restrictions, which is what makes the resulting cost function
  **directed** — `dist(a,b) ≠ dist(b,a)`.
- `strongly=True` is the load-bearing flag. The *weakly* connected component would contain node pairs
  with no legal directed route; truncating to the largest **strongly**-connected component guarantees
  every shortest-path query terminates. Without it, [[lazy-dijkstra-distance-cache]] would need an
  unreachable-pair code path.
- Parallel edges (OSM regularly has several ways between the same node pair) are collapsed to the
  shortest directed length, so the C++ side reads a simple graph.

The graph then leaves Python entirely as `{city}_nodes.csv` and `{city}_edges.csv` — the C++ solver
re-implements Dijkstra rather than calling back into Python. See [[two-program-csv-contract]].

## The reproducibility finding

**OSM is a live database, so an OSMnx download is not a fixed input.** Everything else in the pipeline
is seeded and deterministic; the map is not, and the repo measured exactly how much that costs:

> "Re-running the deterministic `greedy` on a freshly downloaded Wrocław graph gave 178,207 / 322,318
> / 458,921 m vs the paper's 177,555 / 299,944 / 481,089 m — same demands and capacity, but a
> different sampled road graph (OSM has drifted; today's largest SCC = 3,893 nodes)."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/docs/DATA_VERIFICATION.md, 2026-07-09

Note the direction of the drift is not uniform — one instance got shorter, two got longer. This is
the reason the frozen solver reports are committed while the instance and graph CSVs are gitignored:
the artefact is the reference, the regeneration is not. It also means the {{operator-bake-off}} cannot
be re-run to the same numbers.

**The practical lesson:** any pipeline whose first stage hits a live public dataset should commit the
downloaded snapshot, not just the code that downloads it. This repo committed the downstream results
instead, which preserves the paper but not the experiment.

## Dependency hygiene

`requirements.txt` pins only `osmnx>=2.0`, leaves `networkx`, `pandas` and `numpy` unpinned, and
**omits `matplotlib` entirely** although `plot_analysis.py` imports it — see [[matplotlib]] and
[[documentation-drift]]. A clean install from that file cannot produce the figures.
